FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the basic elements of an effective physical examination of the shoulder joint.
Use physical examination findings, including active versus passive range of motion and
strength testing, to discern between various types of shoulder pathology.
Employ special tests to further characterize shoulder pathology.
Recognize crossover etiologies of shoulder pain, including pathologies of the cervical spine,
brachial plexus, and vascular origins.
Overview
Physical examination of the shoulder is a critical component of patient evaluation.

Special tests
Physical examination should be used in combination with patient history and imaging studies
to determine a diagnosis.
Patient History
The patient history should characterize:
Onset: acute versus chronic
Duration of symptoms
Presence of injury/trauma
Associated symptoms: swelling, erythema, paresthesias, weakness
Provoking or palliating factors or treatments
Trend of symptoms
The detailed history of a patient with a shoulder problem also should include:
Handedness
Occupation
Goals of treatment (activities, hobbies)
Prior surgical procedures
Prior nonsurgical treatment
Draping/Patient Positioning

Draping/Patient Positioning
The patient should be draped appropriately to allow circumferential visualization of the
sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular, glenohumeral, scapulothoracic, and scapular surface
anatomy bilaterally. This is most effectively achieved with the use of an examination

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000614
2/36

gown. Surgeons should maintain and respect patients’ cultural beliefs and modesty
throughout the physical examination.
General Inspection

General Inspection
The patient’s general posture, bone and/or soft-tissue deformity, prior incisions and
scars, regions of swelling or erythema, muscle atrophy, and asymmetry should be
carefully noted. The scapulae are examined bilaterally for resting attitude and
winging/dyskinesia with movement of the shoulder through its range of motion (ROM).
Gait Evaluation
Shoulder examination should include gait evaluation to evaluate for symmetric and reciprocal
use of the upper extremities.
Palpation
Anatomic landmarks of the shoulder:
Bone landmarks are critical for examiners orienting themselves for physical examination.
Acromion
Acromioclavicular joint
Coracoid process
Scapular spine
Sternoclavicular joint
Greater tuberosity
Lesser tuberosity
Bicipital groove
Soft-tissue landmarks of the shoulder
Biceps tendon

Periscapular soft tissues: Palpation of the supraspinatus fossa and infraspinatus fossa may
reveal small amounts of atrophy that may be difficult to identify on inspection. The scapular
margins can be palpated in patients with periscapular pain.
ROM Tests
Active ROM of the shoulder is initially assessed with the patient in the upright position. The
following movements are observed: forward elevation, abduction, external rotation (with the
arm adducted), and internal rotation behind the back (Table 1). To isolate glenohumeral
motion, horizontal adduction and internal and external rotation in 90° of abduction are
measured with the patient in the supine position or with the examiner’s hand stabilizing the
scapula.

Both shoulders are examined simultaneously, and differences in their rhythm and maximum
ROM are noted.
Passive ROM of the glenohumeral joint is observed, and limitations or, less commonly,
increased passive movements are noted. These values may vary widely among patients, and

comparison of shoulder motion with that of the normal contralateral shoulder is
advantageous.
Associated scapulothoracic motion also is evaluated, with the patient standing and with
observation of elevation, depression, protraction, and retraction during shoulder elevation and
lowering in the scapular and sagittal planes.

ROM Tests
Scapular dyskinesia often is an under-recognized contributor of shoulder pain and
should be evaluated during the standard examination of the shoulder. Scapular
dyskinesia can be assessed by stabilizing the patient’s clavicle and asking the patient to
repeatedly forward elevate his or her shoulder to maximum flexion, perform a wall
push-up, or abduct. Any asymmetry in motion of the medial border of the scapula is
considered a positive test, which is associated with a sensitivity of 0.78 and a specificity
of 0.76. Lateral scapular winging is defined by excessive lateral rotation or increased
distance between the borders of each scapula. Medial scapular winging is defined by a
prominent inferior scapular tip with asymmetric medial prominence during shoulder
motion. To aid in the diagnosis, relief of symptoms via manual medial stabilization can
be performed. Assessment of the gross muscle bulk of the serratus anterior and
trapezius also should be noted because they may contribute to medial and lateral
scapular winging, respectively1 (Resource 1).
Strength Tests
To assess rotator cuff strength, the patient is examined in the standing position, with the
scapulae in a retracted and depressed position. Each muscle unit of the rotator cuff is isolated
and tested in sequence. Power is graded according to the Medical Research Council rating
scale (Table 2).

The empty can (Jobe) test is performed with the shoulder in 70° to 90° of abduction in the
plane of the scapula and in internal rotation, with the forearm maximally pronated.
Downward pressure is applied to the forearm, which the patient is asked to resist (Figure
1). A positive test has been described as pain and/or weakness. Pain alone is not indicative
of the degree of rotator cuff pathology; however, additional weakness may be a sign of
more considerable rotator cuff pathology, such as a full-thickness tear. The full can test is
performed in manner similar to that of the Jobe test, except the humerus is externally
rotated 45°, simulating the position a person would hold a full can.2-5

pp 727-741.)
The champagne toast test is performed with the shoulder in 30° of abduction in the plane
of the scapula, 30° of forward elevation, and mild external rotation. The patient is asked to
resist downward pressure applied to the upper arm. This position better isolates the
abducting function of the supraspinatus from that of the deltoid.
The drop arm test is performed by having the patient actively abduct his or her shoulder to
90° and then slowly lower the arm. A positive test occurs if the patient cannot lower the
arm slowly and instead drops the arm immediately because of pain.6
The painful arc test is performed by passively elevating the patient’s arm to 180° and then
letting the patient actively lower the arm in the abduction plane. A positive test occurs if the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:23 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000614
8/36

pain is minimal at full elevation but increases as the arm lowers to 90° and is maximal with
the arm between 70° and 120° of abduction.4,7
The infraspinatus and teres minor muscles are primarily external rotators of the shoulder,
and strength testing can be isolated by varying the level of shoulder abduction. Diagnostic
accuracy of these tests is shown in Table 4.
The infraspinatus muscle is tested with the shoulder abducted 20° in the scapular plane
and the elbow in 90° of flexion. The patient attempts to externally rotate the arm from 45°
of internal rotation against the examiner’s counterforce (Figure 2). If the patient is unable
to do so, the examiner positions the arm at 5° less than maximal passive external rotation
to allow for capsular recoil and asks the patient to hold the arm in this position as the wrist
is released. If the patient’s arm spontaneously falls back by more than 10° of internal
rotation, the result is designated a positive external rotation lag or dropping sign, indicating
insufficiency of the infraspinatus muscle.8,9
The teres minor muscle is isolated with the patient’s elbow flexed to 90° and the arm in 90°
of external rotation and 90° of abduction. Power is tested as the examiner attempts to
forcibly rotate the arm internally from its abducted and externally rotated position. If any
weakness is perceived, the shoulder is passively placed in the above position and the
patient is asked to maintain the arm in that position against gravity. Inability to do so,
defined by spontaneous internal rotation of the shoulder, is considered a positive
hornblower sign, indicating teres minor insufficiency.4,9

The belly-press maneuver is performed with the patient’s hand pressing on the upper
abdomen and the elbow anterior to the wrist in the coronal plane. The power of the press
and any tendency of the elbow to fall behind the wrist are noted. This test is graded
negative if the patient can push the hand against the stomach with the wrist fully extended.
The test is graded positive if the elbow is unable to circumduct the plane of the wrist on the
abdomen because this indicates subscapularis deficiency with compensation from the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:23 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Shoulder
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000614
11/36

posterior deltoid.10,11 The belly-press test is associated with a sensitivity and specificity of
0.28 to 0.50 and 0.96 to 0.99, respectively.12
The lift-off test is performed with the shoulder rotated internally and the dorsum of the
patient’s hand resting against the ipsilateral sacroiliac joint. To ensure that the patient is
not limited by internal joint stiffness, the examiner passively positions the back of the
patient’s hand away from the sacroiliac region and asks the patient to maintain that
position. The patient’s power in lifting the back of the hand against resistance from that
position should be noted.10 The lift-off maneuver is associated with a sensitivity of 0.12 to
0.25 and a specificity of 0.95 to 1.00.12
The bear-hug test requires the patient to place the palm of the hand on the opposite
shoulder, with the elbow anterior to the body. The patient maintains an internal rotation
force in this position as the examiner attempts to externally rotate the patient’s arm.
Weakness of the arm compared with the arm on the contralateral side is considered a
positive test, indicating a tear in the upper border of the subscapularis muscle or tendon11
(Figure 3). The bear-hug test is associated with a sensitivity and specificity of 0.19 to 0.60
and 0.81 to 0.92, respectively.12

Strength Tests
Combining positive test results can increase the likelihood ratios and post-test
probabilities of a partial-thickness or full-thickness rotator cuff tear. Weakness in
external rotation and on the Jobe test, a positive Neer sign or Hawkins-Kennedy
impingement test, or having two of these positive tests in addition to being older than 60
years is associated with a 98% likelihood of a rotator cuff tear.13,14 A positive result in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:23 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Shoulder
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000614
13/36

the painful arc and drop-arm tests and weakness in external rotation is associated with a
likelihood ratio 1 of 15.6 and a 91% likelihood of a full-thickness rotator cuff tear.13
Conversely, if all three of these tests were negative, the likelihood ratio 2 and likelihood
of a full-thickness rotator cuff tear are very low, at 0.16 and 9%, respectively.13
Provocative Tests/Special Tests
Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD)/internal impingement in throwers is a pathology
defined as loss, in degrees, of internal rotation of the glenohumeral joint in the affected
(throwing) shoulder compared with the nonaffected shoulder. This loss is measured as the
difference in internal rotation in abduction with the scapula stabilized.
The loss of internal rotation relates to a concomitant posterior capsular contracture, and
external rotation often is increased with attenuation of the anterior capsule and
glenohumeral ligaments. As the contracture evolves, the center of rotation of the humeral
head shifts superiorly and posteriorly, which may result in impingement of the labrum and
rotator cuff between the greater tuberosity and the glenoid if the arm is abducted and
excessively externally rotated (internal impingement).
This internal impingement may result in partial articular-sided tears of the rotator cuff and
superior labrum anterior to posterior (SLAP) lesions and should be evaluated in throwers
with shoulder pain. Shoulders with a GIRD of more than 20° compared with GIRD of the
contralateral shoulder are considered at risk for injury.

Provocative Tests/Special Tests
Knowledge of GIRD continues to evolve. In high-volume overhead throwers, the
posterior capsule becomes scarred and tightened in response to the tremendous
deceleration forces the shoulder experiences. Conversely, the anterior capsule becomes
attenuated. Clinically, this manifests as loss of internal rotation with the shoulder in
abduction. Typically, an internal rotation deficit of 20° is required for a diagnosis of GIRD;
however, changes in the glenohumeral center of rotation and kinematics may occur in
with as little as 5° of GIRD.15 In addition, bony anatomic abnormalities may be observed
in patients with this condition. In youth and adolescent baseball players, clinical loss of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:23 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000614
14/36

internal rotation has been attributed to increased proximal humeral retroversion, which
may be a compensatory anatomic change in skeletally immature throwers and not
necessarily pathologic in this patient population.16 However, in professional pitchers
GIRD correlates with a higher rate of shoulder injuries and progression toward SLAP and
articular-sided rotator cuff tears.17
Impingement
In the Neer impingement test, the patient’s scapula is stabilized and the arm is passively taken
through a full arc of forward elevation. In terminal forward elevation, pain is experienced at
the anterior edge of the acromion and may indicate subacromial impingement syndrome or
rotator cuff pathology. The diagnosis is confirmed if the pain is relieved by injecting 10 mL of
1% xylocaine beneath the anterior acromion (Figure 4). The specificity and sensitivity of this
physical examination maneuver are 0.59 and 0.60, respectively.

In the Hawkins-Kennedy test, the examiner positions the patient’s arm in internal rotation in
90° of abduction in the scapular plane. Pain in this position may indicate subacromial
impingement syndrome or rotator cuff pathology, with the greater tuberosity pressed against
the coracoacromial ligament and the acromion (Figure 5). Similar to the Neer test, this physical
examination test has a specificity and specificity of 0.58 and 0.67, respectively.3

Acromioclavicular Joint
Acromioclavicular joint injury and instability may be associated with pain about the
acromioclavicular joint. Gravity-assisted arm traction may accentuate joint deformity and
vertical instability compared with the contralateral shoulder, which is indicative of injury to the
coracoclavicular ligaments. Pain without joint deformity may be indicative of injury to the
acromioclavicular joint while sparing the coracoclavicular ligaments. The acromioclavicular
joint instability test is performed by palpating a gap in the acromioclavicular joint. Gross
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:23 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Shoulder
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000614
17/36

instability of the acromioclavicular joint with manual maneuvers is indicative of higher grade
injuries.
In the cross-arm adduction test, the patient’s arm is brought into 90° of forward elevation and
maximal adduction, producing axial compression across the acromioclavicular joint. Pain at
the acromioclavicular joint may indicate degenerative pathology. If performed with the patient
in the supine position and the scapula stabilized, this also is a test for posterior capsular
tightness. Pain at the posterior aspect of the glenohumeral joint, with a diminished ROM
compared with that on the contralateral side indicates symptomatic contracture (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Photograph shows the cross-arm test for degenerative pathology of the
acromioclavicular joint. (Reproduced from Matache BA, Gammon B, Athwal GS, Bicknell RT:
Physical examination of the shoulder and elbow, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
727-741.)
The Paxinos test is performed with the patient’s arm relaxed at the side of the body. The
examiner then creates a shearing force across the acromioclavicular joint by applying thumb
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:23 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Shoulder
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000614
18/36

pressure over the posterior acromion and counterpressure with the index finger over the
distal clavicle. Pain at the acromioclavicular joint may indicate degenerative changes in the
joint.
Provocative tests of the acromioclavicular joint are, individually, of low sensitivity; however, a
combination of the Paxinos test, cross-arm test, and acromioclavicular instability test is
associated with a specificity of 0.9.18
SLAP Tear
Clinical diagnosis of SLAP tears remains a challenge because any long head of the biceps (LHB)
pathology or maneuvers that aggravate the LHB may masquerade as SLAP pathology. Each of
these examination maneuvers is associated with a unique sensitivity and specificity, such that
if examination maneuvers are performed in combination, they can result in improved
diagnostic accuracy.
The O’Brien test (also called the active compression test) is performed with the patient’s arm in
90° of forward elevation, with the elbow in full extension, full internal rotation of the shoulder
(thumb pointed down), and 10° to 15° of adduction. The examiner applies a downward force
to the forearm that is resisted by the patient. Pain in the glenohumeral joint that is absent if
the test is repeated with the shoulder in maximum external rotation (forearm supinated)
indicates a SLAP tear (Figure 7). The O’Brien test is associated with a specificity of 0.36 and a
sensitivity of 0.66 for the accurate diagnosis of SLAP tears.3 Therefore, confirmation via other
physical examination maneuvers and imaging studies is prudent.

adduction. The examiner applies a downward force to the forearm that is resisted by the

Physical examination of the shoulder and elbow, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
727-741.)
In the crank test, the patient is seated and the examiner positions the patient’s arm in 160° of
forward elevation in the scapular plane. The glenohumeral joint is axially loaded in this
position along the axis of the humerus, with passive internal and external rotation of the
humerus. Pain, particularly in external rotation of the humerus and with a catching sensation,
indicates a SLAP tear (Figure 8). The crank test is associated with a specificity of 0.72 and a
sensitivity 0.46.3

In the dynamic labral shear test, the examiner flexes the patient’s elbow to 90° and abducts
the arm to 120° while maximally externally rotating the arm. While placing the arm in maximal
horizontal abduction and maintaining external rotation of the arm, the examiner lowers the
arm to 60° of abduction. A positive test occurs with pain and/or a painful click along the
posterior joint line between 120° and 90° of abduction. The dynamic labral shear test is
associated with a sensitivity of 0.78 and a specificity of 0.51.19
The biceps load test 2 is used to assess potentially isolated SLAP pathology, in contrast to the
biceps load test 1, which is designed for patients with anterior shoulder instability and a SLAP
tear. In the biceps load test 2, the patient is in supine position and the arm is placed in 120° of
forward elevation and maximal external rotation. With the elbow in 90° of flexion, the forearm
is supinated. The patient is asked to flex the elbow, with the examiner resisting this flexion. If
this increases pain beyond its baseline severity, the test result is positive.
In the anterior slide test, the patient is examined in the standing or sitting position with the
hands on the hips and the thumbs pointed posteriorly. The examiner’s hand cups the superior
aspect of the patient’s shoulder, with the tip of the examiner’s index finger extending over the
anterior aspect of the patient’s acromion. The examiner’s contralateral hand then applies a
force to the patient’s elbow, driving the humeral head anteriorly and superiorly. The patient is
asked to resist this force. Pain and/or a click emanating from the front of the shoulder
constitutes a positive test result.
Pathology of the LHB
In the Speed test, the patient’s arm is placed at 90° of forward elevation in the sagittal plane,
with the elbow extended and the forearm supinated. A downward force is applied to the
forearm, and pain in the anterior shoulder indicates pathology of the LHB tendon (Figure 9).
The Speed test is associated with a specificity of 0.88 and a sensitivity of 0.20.3

The three-pack test combines the O’Brien (active compression) test, throwing test, and bicipital
tunnel palpation. The throwing test is performed with the elbow flexed 90° and the shoulder
abducted 90° in the scapular plane and in maximal external rotation (late cocking position).
The examiner provides resistance to the arm as the patient steps forward with the
contralateral leg (early acceleration position). Pain with this maneuver indicates a positive
result. Pain with each component of the three-pack test is highly indicative of pathology of the
LHB tendon. Pain with the throwing motion, the O’Brien test, and anterior biceps pain (the
three elements of this examination) is associated with a sensitivity of 0.73 to 0.98 and a
specificity of 0.46 to 0.79.20

An overall assessment of ligamentous laxity is crucial for diagnosing shoulder instability.
Patients with multidirectional instability attributed to a generalized patholaxity, such as Ehlers-
Danlos syndrome, fall into a unique treatment category, and surgeons should identify these
patients before proceeding with surgical management. The Beighton scoring system is useful
for quantifying the amount of generalized ligamentous laxity. Signs of this may include
hyperextension at the elbows and knees, ability to place the palms of the hands on the floor
with the knees extended, and ability to bring the thumbs to the forearm. Excessive translation
of the humeral head on the glenoid in this scenario may not be pathologic if it does not cause
pain or diminish function.
The load-and-shift test can be performed with the patient in the supine position. The
examiner holds the shoulder in 20° of abduction and forward flexion to center the humeral
head with the scapular plane. The examiner then applies an anteriorly and posteriorly
directed force. The modified Hawkins grading system can be used to determine the degree
of translation (Table 6; Figure 11). This maneuver is associated with a sensitivity of 0.72 and
a specificity of 0.90.19

Figure 11 Photograph shows the modified load-and-shift test for anterior and posterior

The sulcus sign is measured by placing downward axial traction on the arm with the patient
seated upright and the shoulder in a neutral position at the side. A sulcus, or dimple between
the humeral head and the lateral edge of the acromion, is suggestive of inferior instability
and/or generalized laxity. A type I sulcus is less than 1 cm of translation, a type II sulcus is 1
to 2 cm of translation, and a type III sulcus is greater than 2 cm of translation. A comparison
should be made with the findings on examination of the contralateral shoulder (Figure 12).
The maneuver should be repeated with the shoulder in 30° of external rotation. The test is
considered positive if inferior translation persists in 30° of external rotation. No literature is
available on the accuracy, specificity, or sensitivity of this maneuver.19

Posterior instability—Posterior instability can be examined via the posterior jerk test.
The posterior jerk test is performed with the patient seated and the shoulder forward
flexed to 90° and 90° of internal rotation. An axial load is applied with a posterior directed
force to the humerus. As the examiner forces the shoulder posterior and then abducts the
shoulder to 90°, the feeling of reduction, or clunk, as the humeral head reduces is
indicative of a positive test. This test is associated with a specificity ranging from 0.85 to
0.98 and a sensitivity ranging from 0.73 to 0.90.19

Neurovascular Examination

Neurovascular Examination
Shoulder pathology, especially trauma, may compromise the neurovascular status of a
patient’s upper extremity. Conversely, neurologic conditions, commonly cervical spine
pathology, may mimic shoulder pathology. Therefore, clinical evaluation of patients with
shoulder problems should include a neurovascular assessment of both upper
extremities for comparison. The brachial, radial, and ulnar pulses can be palpated to
assess for adequate vascular perfusion. The integrity of the patient’s peripheral nerves
can be assessed by testing the strength and sensation of the upper extremity (Table 7).

Other Tests

Cervical Spine
A comprehensive examination of the shoulder should include a detailed neurologic
examination if a patient’s symptoms of pain or paresthesias radiate to the medial
scapula or below the elbow. The examination should include an evaluation of ROM of
the cervical spine; evaluation of neck pain; performance of the Spurling maneuver;
performance of the shoulder abduction test; and evaluation of myotomal strength,
dermatomal sensation, and reflexes if indicated. The Spurling maneuver is performed by
gently extending the neck, tilting the head toward the suspected side, and gently axially
loading the head/neck. The appearance or exacerbation of radicular symptoms is a
positive result. The shoulder abduction test is performed with the patient sitting and
lifting his or her hand overhead. A positive result is a decrease or elimination of radicular
symptoms.21 (Resource 2).


Thoracic Outlet Syndrome
The Roos test (the elevated arm stress test) is a reliable diagnostic examination for
thoracic outlet syndrome. In this maneuver, the patient places both arms in the 90°
abducted position with the elbows flexed to 90°. The hands are then opened and closed
for a 3-minute period. Minor discomfort because of muscular fatigue is a normal
response; however, patients with thoracic outlet syndrome have more dramatic
symptoms that replicate their usual discomfort to the extent that they may not be able
to complete the test.22
Imaging Studies
Physical examination findings should be correlated with plain radiographs and should inform
clinical decisions to pursue additional imaging studies. Depending on patient presentation and
history, specialized radiographs, MRI, ultrasonography, CT, and other imaging modalities may
be clinically helpful.
